title: Energy, Energy Transfer & General Energy Analysis
source: Cengel, Boles & Kanoglu — Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach, Ch. 2
summary:
Energy comes in many **forms**, and thermodynamics groups them in two ways. *Macroscopic* energy is energy the whole system has relative to some outside frame — **kinetic energy** $KE = \tfrac12 mV^2$ from motion and **potential energy** $PE = mgz$ from elevation. *Microscopic* energy is the energy of the molecules themselves; summed up, it is the **internal energy** $U$. Together these make the **total energy** $E = U + KE + PE$. In most closed-system problems the system isn't moving or changing height, so only $U$ changes.

Energy crosses a boundary in just three ways: **heat**, **work**, and (for open systems) **mass flow**. **Heat** $Q$ is energy transfer driven by a temperature difference; **work** $W$ is every other organized energy transfer (a moving piston, a rotating shaft, electric current, a spring). Both are *transfers*, not properties — a system contains energy, never "heat" or "work". A process with no heat transfer is **adiabatic**.

The sign convention used here (the formal one): heat *added to* the system is positive, work *done by* the system is positive. The unifying statement is the **first law**, written as an **energy balance**: $E_{in} - E_{out} = \Delta E_{system}$. Energy is never created or destroyed, only converted or moved across the boundary. The rate form, $\dot E_{in} - \dot E_{out} = dE_{system}/dt$, is what you use for power and flow problems.

Some work modes recur constantly: **electrical work** $W_e = VI\,\Delta t$, **shaft work** $W_{sh} = 2\pi n T$ (a torque turning at $n$ revolutions), boundary work (Ch 4), and spring work. The **mechanical energy** of a flowing fluid — the part that can be fully converted to work by an ideal device — is $e_{mech} = P/\rho + V^2/2 + gz$, the basis for pump and turbine analysis.

Finally, real devices waste energy, captured by **efficiency**. Thermal efficiency relates useful output to energy input; mechanical/pump/turbine and motor/generator efficiencies chain together multiplicatively for a combined device. Efficiency is where the *quality* of energy (Ch 6) first shows up: you never get all of a high-temperature heat input back as work.

equations.name: Total energy & its parts
equations.latex: E = U + KE + PE, \qquad e = u + \frac{V^2}{2} + gz
equations.useWhen: Setting up any energy balance. For a stationary closed system $\Delta KE = \Delta PE = 0$, so $\Delta E = \Delta U$ — the usual simplification.
equations.note: Lower-case $e, u$ are per-unit-mass (specific) energies; multiply by $m$ for totals.

equations.name: Energy balance (first law)
equations.useWhen: The master equation for *every* thermodynamics problem. Start here, then cancel the terms that are zero for your specific system.
equations.note: Sign convention: $Q$ in is +, $W$ out is +. Units: kJ.

equations.name: Rate form (power)
equations.useWhen: Anything stated as a rate or power (kW), or any steady-operation device. At steady state the right-hand side is zero.
equations.note: A dot means "per unit time": $\dot Q$ in kW, $\dot W$ in kW, $\dot m$ in kg/s.

equations.name: Electrical work
equations.useWhen: A resistor, heater, or electric device is inside the system. $\dot W_e = VI$ gives the instantaneous power.
equations.note: $V$ = voltage, $I$ = current. This is work done *on* the system (negative in the by-system convention).

equations.name: Shaft work
equations.useWhen: A rotating shaft transmits power — fans, turbines, mixers. $\dot n$ is revolutions per unit time, $T$ is torque.
equations.note: Watch units: if $\dot n$ is in rev/s and $T$ in N·m, $\dot W_{sh}$ comes out in W.

equations.name: Mechanical energy of a flow
equations.useWhen: Pumps, turbines, hydro and wind problems — the fully-convertible (work-grade) part of a fluid's energy.
equations.note: No thermal term: mechanical energy excludes internal energy, which can't be fully turned into work.

equations.name: Efficiency (general & combined)
equations.useWhen: Converting between an ideal (reversible) amount of work and the real machine's input/output, or chaining device efficiencies (e.g. motor × pump).
equations.note: Always < 1 for real devices. Multiply component efficiencies for an overall figure.

glossary.definition: All energy a system holds: $E = U + KE + PE$. On a per-mass basis, $e = u + V^2/2 + gz$.
The sum of all microscopic energies (molecular translation, rotation, vibration, intermolecular forces). A property of the system.
Macroscopic energies from motion ($KE = \tfrac12 mV^2$) and elevation ($PE = mgz$), measured relative to an external reference.
Energy transferred across a boundary purely because of a temperature difference. A transfer, not a stored quantity.
Any organized energy transfer across a boundary that is not heat — boundary, shaft, electrical, spring work, etc.
A process with no heat transfer ($Q = 0$), either because the system is insulated or because it happens too fast.
Energy transfer per unit time (kW). Denoted with a dot: $\dot W$, $\dot Q$.
Conservation of energy: $E_{in} - E_{out} = \Delta E_{system}$. The backbone of every analysis.
The portion of a fluid's energy that an ideal device can fully convert to work: $P/\rho + V^2/2 + gz$. Excludes internal energy.
Net work output divided by heat input, $\eta_{th} = W_{net,out}/Q_{in}$. Capped below 1 by the second law.
Heat *into* the system is positive; work *done by* the system is positive. Be consistent across the whole problem.

tips: **Start every problem with the energy balance** $E_{in}-E_{out}=\Delta E_{system}$, then strike out the zero terms. It stops you from guessing which formula to use.
**Heat and work are transfers, not properties.** A system never "contains heat". It contains energy ($U$); heat and work are how that energy crosses the boundary.
**Drop $\Delta KE$ and $\Delta PE$ unless told otherwise.** For most closed systems they're negligible next to $\Delta U$ — but state the assumption.
**Keep one sign convention.** Mixing "work in positive" with "work out positive" mid-problem is a classic source of sign errors. The book uses: $Q$ in +, $W$ out +.
**Check the units bridge.** Power in kW × time in s = kJ; $1\ \text{kPa·m}^3 = 1\ \text{kJ}$; $V\cdot I$ in volts·amps = watts.
